title: Capstone: A Passage, Its Readers and Your Argument
bigQuestion: What does one passage mean to its readers, why do they read it differently, and how can you make a careful argument about it?

story.title: The Same First Word
story.kicker: A student lays out three commentaries on one verse and finds they all begin with the same word.
paragraphs: Jalen has chosen Bhagavad Gita 18.66 for his capstone. He has printed three readings and laid them side by side on the library table: a summary of Shankara's commentary, a summary of Ramanuja's, and a passage from Gandhi's letters on the Gita. He has also printed the verse itself in Telang's prose translation of 1882.

As he reads, he notices something. All three readings begin in the same place: the first word of the verse, sarvadharman, "all dharmas." What does it mean to give up all dharmas? Shankara's school reads it as giving up the sense of being the doer of actions. Ramanuja's school reads it as giving up reliance on any means except surrender to God. Gandhi reads it as giving up selfish attachment while still doing one's work.

Jalen realizes that the disagreement is not random. Each reader brings a whole view of the self, God and action to that one word. Shankara holds that the self is not other than Brahman. Ramanuja holds that the self depends wholly on a loving God. Gandhi is a man in the middle of a political struggle who believes in nonviolent action.

His teacher had told the class that a capstone is not a report. It is an argument about what a passage has meant to its readers, and why. Jalen starts to write his thesis: the three readings of 18.66 differ because each reader's view of the self decides what "giving up" can mean.

In this chapter you will go through the same steps: choose a passage, establish its text and translation, set its context, gather three readings, build an argument, cite exactly and attribute every belief, and present your work to others.
story.think: Jalen notices that all three readers begin with the same word. Why might a single word be the place where readings split apart?

lessons.title: Choosing a Passage
lessons.mainIdea: A good capstone passage is short, much discussed and read in more than one way by named readers.
reading: Your first task is to choose one passage. Good choices are short enough to read closely but rich enough to have many readers. Options from this course include a Gita verse (2.47, 4.7–4.8, 9.26, 11.32 or 18.66), an Upanishad dialogue (Katha 1.3.3–4 or Chandogya 6.12–6.13), a Rig Veda hymn (10.129 or 10.90), or an epic episode (Draupadi's question or Sita's return to the earth).

Ask three questions before you decide. Can I find at least three different readings by named people or schools? Is there a public-domain translation I can quote exactly, such as Telang, Arnold, Müller, Griffith or Ganguli? Does the passage raise a question I care about? A passage that meets all three will carry your project.

Avoid passages that are very long, like a whole book, or so obscure that you cannot find readers. It also helps to choose a *focused question*. "What does the Gita mean?" is too big. "How have readers understood 'giving up all dharmas' in Gita 18.66?" is focused enough to answer well.

words.d: a final project that brings together the skills of a course
a narrow research question that can be answered with evidence
a short section of a text chosen for close study

lessons.title: Establishing the Text
lessons.mainIdea: Before arguing, state exactly which text, verse and translation you use, and note any important differences between versions.
reading: Scholars begin by "establishing the text": saying exactly what words they are reading. For your capstone, give the text's name, the chapter and verse or episode, and the translation with its year. For example: "Chandogya Upanishad 6.8.7, translated by F. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East 1 (1879)."

If you can, compare two translations. Note where they differ in an important word. For Gita 2.47, Telang's "your business is with action alone" and Arnold's verse render the same Sanskrit very differently. If a Sanskrit word is at the center of your question, like sarvadharman or tat tvam asi, give it with a plain gloss.

For epics, note which version you mean: Valmiki's Ramayana, Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas or another retelling. Scholars also point out that the Mahabharata and Ramayana exist in many manuscripts, and that the *critical editions* made in Pune and Baroda compare them. You do not need to read manuscripts, but you should know that the text has a history.

words.d: stating exactly which words, version and translation one is reading
a scholarly text built by comparing many manuscripts
a short explanation of a word's meaning

lessons.title: Setting the Context
lessons.mainIdea: Context means the passage's place in its text, its speaker and listener, and its date, both scholarly and traditional.
reading: Context has layers. First, *literary context*: where does the passage sit in the larger text? Gita 18.66 comes near the end, after all the teaching, just before Arjuna says his doubt is gone. That placement matters. Second, the speakers: who says it, to whom, and in what situation? Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield.

Third, *historical context*: when was the text composed, and in what world? Give both kinds of date. Scholars date the Gita to about the 2nd century BCE to the 2nd century CE. Hindu tradition places the war at the start of the Kali Yuga, often given as 3102 BCE. Name both, and say who holds each.

Finally, context includes the readers. Each reader you will study also had a setting: Shankara in 8th-century India, Ramanuja at Srirangam, Gandhi in a colonial prison. A short paragraph on context shows your audience that you understand the passage before you argue about it.

words.d: where a passage sits in its larger text
the time and world in which a text was composed
in Hindu tradition, the present age of the world, often dated from 3102 BCE

lessons.title: Gathering Three Readings
lessons.mainIdea: Gather a classical commentator, a modern reader and a scholar, and state each reading in words its holder would accept.
reading: Your capstone gathers three readings. One should be a *classical commentator*, such as Shankara, Ramanuja or Madhva. One should be a modern reader, such as Vivekananda, Tilak, Gandhi, Aurobindo or Ambedkar. One should be a scholar of religion who studies the passage historically. You may add a devotional reader, a poet or a community voice.

Commentaries are not in the public domain in most English versions, so paraphrase them and name the source you used. Modern readers' own words, such as Gandhi's letters, may also need paraphrase. Keep a simple chart: reader, date, setting, what they say the passage means, and the reasons they give.

The key skill is *charity*: stating each reading so fairly that its holder would recognize it. Do not make a reading sound foolish so yours looks better. If you disagree with a reader, first state the reading at its strongest, as the Sanskrit commentators did with the purvapaksha.

words.d: a premodern writer of a formal commentary, such as Shankara or Ramanuja
in reading, stating others' views as fairly and strongly as they would
restating a passage in one's own words

lessons.title: Why Readers Differ
lessons.mainIdea: Readers differ because of their schools, settings, questions and methods, and naming these reasons is the heart of your analysis.
reading: Once you have three readings, ask why they differ. Scholars often point to four causes. First, *school*: a reader's tradition, such as Advaita or Sri Vaishnava, shapes what a passage can mean. Second, setting: a reader in prison under colonial rule asks different questions than a monk in a monastery.

Third, the question the reader brings: a reformer asking about caste reads Gita 4.13 differently from a devotee asking about God. Fourth, method: a commentator reads word by word and within the whole of scripture; a historian reads the passage in the world of its composition; a poet reads for image and feeling.

Naming these causes turns a list of opinions into analysis. Instead of saying "Shankara thinks X and Gandhi thinks Y," you can say "Shankara reads X because his view of the self requires it, while Gandhi reads Y because he was asking how to act without violence." That "because" is where your argument lives.

words.d: explaining how and why something works, not just describing it
the way a reader approaches a text
the main claim an essay argues

look.title: Adding "Because"
look.text: List: "Madhva reads tat tvam asi as difference. Shankara reads it as identity." Analysis: "Madhva reads difference because his theology holds God and souls are eternally distinct, and he supports it by dividing the Sanskrit as atat; Shankara reads identity because he holds the self is not other than Brahman."

check.why: School, setting, question and method shape readings.

check.q: What turns a list of opinions into analysis?

check.q: What is a thesis?

lessons.title: Building the Argument
lessons.mainIdea: A strong capstone states a thesis about why readings differ, supports it with cited evidence and answers an objection.
reading: Your *thesis* is one or two sentences that answer your focused question. For example: "Readers of Gita 18.66 differ mainly because each one's view of the self decides what 'giving up all dharmas' can mean." A good thesis can be argued; someone could disagree with it.

Each body paragraph should present one reading, with a citation, and connect it back to the thesis. Use a clear pattern: claim, evidence, explanation. Claim what the reader says; give the evidence from the text or commentary; explain how it supports your thesis. Keep sentences short and each paragraph on one idea.

Then answer a *counterargument*. Perhaps someone would say the readings differ mainly because of politics, not views of the self. State that objection fairly and respond with evidence. Ending with a counterargument shows that you have thought about other views, which is the same habit the classical commentators practiced.

words.d: an objection to one's thesis, stated fairly and answered
a pattern for body paragraphs
quoted or paraphrased passages and facts that support a claim

lessons.title: Citing and Attributing
lessons.mainIdea: Every quotation needs an exact citation, and every belief needs to be attributed to the person or tradition who holds it.
reading: In this course, two habits matter most. First, *cite exactly*. Every quotation names the text, chapter and verse, translator and year. Quote exactly only from public-domain translations like Telang, Arnold, Müller, Griffith or Ganguli. For all others, paraphrase in your own words and still cite the source.

Second, *attribute every belief*. Write "Vaishnava readers understand Krishna as an avatar of Vishnu," not "Krishna is an avatar of Vishnu." Write "Shankara holds that the self is Brahman," not "the self is Brahman." Attribution keeps your essay descriptive and fair, and it lets readers of every background trust it.

Attribution is not the same as having no opinion. You may argue about what a passage means to its readers and why. What you should not do, in a public-school essay, is claim that a religious teaching is true or false. Describe, compare and analyze; do not preach or dismiss.

words.d: naming who holds a belief or reading
no longer under copyright and free to quote
describing what people believe and do, without judging its truth

lessons.title: Presenting to the Class
lessons.mainIdea: A clear presentation shows the passage, the three readings and your thesis, and invites respectful questions.
reading: Your capstone ends with a short presentation to the class. Plan about five minutes. Start by showing the passage on one slide or handout, with its citation. Read it aloud slowly. Then state your focused question and your thesis in one or two sentences.

Next, present each reading briefly, with the reader's name, date and setting, and one line of evidence. A simple chart or three columns can help your audience compare. Then give your analysis: why the readings differ. End with the counterargument and your answer. Keep text on slides short, and speak in plain words.

Invite questions. Classmates may come from many backgrounds, including Hindu families for whom these texts are sacred. Answer respectfully, and it is fine to say, "I don't know; that would be a good next step." A good *presentation* teaches your classmates something about the passage and about how careful reading works.
